week.t: Iceberg A-81, 1,550 km², reaches South Georgia
A sickle and a padlock: Poland’s double-guarded grave
NEO Surveyor’s sunshade and 864 solar cells pass their tests
NASA streamlines two Moon landers for a 2028 landing
RS-25 engine No. 10001 fires for 500 seconds at Stennis
Nikon Small World: mitochondria on the move inside a leaf

tiles.cap: 864 solar cells on a 6-metre sunshade: NASA’s asteroid hunter is nearly built
tiles.nums: solar cells on NEO Surveyor’s sunshade, together making up to 2 kilowatts, the spacecraft’s only power
tiles.p1: NEO Surveyor is the first spacecraft NASA has built specifically to find large numbers of potentially hazardous asteroids and comets. Its sunshade, built by Applied Aerospace in Stockton, California, stands 6 metres tall and 2.4 metres wide at the base: two flat panels joined at an angle of 23.5 degrees. Its main job is to block the Sun’s glare and keep the telescope cool; it also carries 864 solar cells, the spacecraft’s only source of power, which charge the batteries on board.
tiles.p2: NASA blog update Monday 26 October. Launch is no earlier than September 2027. Dark asteroids reflect little visible light but glow in infrared as the Sun warms them, and infrared is what this telescope sees.
deep: The eye

The telescope’s aperture is 50 cm. Two infrared detector arrays each build a 16-megapixel mosaic of the sky. Seeing an object in two infrared bands lets scientists estimate its temperature, and from that, its size.
Looking where ground telescopes can’t

It will watch for objects approaching from the Sun’s direction and for objects leading or trailing Earth’s orbit, places ground-based telescopes struggle with because of the Sun’s glare. It builds on NASA’s NEOWISE telescope.
The road so far

SolAero Technologies in Albuquerque added the 864 cells in January. Environmental testing finished in March at a thermal vacuum facility in El Segundo, California. In May the sunshade was delivered, ahead of schedule, to BAE Systems in Boulder, Colorado, and inspected in a clean room there in July.
Since then
Coarse Sun sensors, which help the spacecraft work out which way it is pointing, and temperature sensors have been fitted, and the solar array has passed its functional and performance tests.

tiles.cap: An engine that will not fly burned for 500 seconds at 111% power, on purpose.
tiles.nums: the hot fire on 21 October, as long as an RS-25 burns during a real launch
tiles.p1: On Wednesday 21 October, teams at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, fired RS-25 engine No. 10001 for about 8.5 minutes, 500 seconds, the same time the engines run during a Space Launch System launch. It ran at 111% power. This engine is a developmental unit that will not be used in flight; its job is data, which goes to NASA and L3Harris Technologies, the prime engine contractor, to improve engine performance and reliability.
tiles.p2: Each Artemis mission uses four RS-25 engines, which together produce up to 2 million pounds of thrust to launch the SLS. Before use, every RS-25 engine is proven flightworthy at Stennis.
deep: What the photo shows

A huge cloud of white vapour rising from the test structure while the engine fires, the flames barely visible through the stand, water filling the foreground. Photo by NASA’s Danny Nowlin; posted 23 October.
Why test an engine that won’t fly
A developmental engine exists to produce data. What NASA and L3Harris learn from No. 10001 goes into improving engine performance and reliability.
Four at once
On a launch, four RS-25 engines fire together, up to 2 million pounds of thrust between them, for the same 500 seconds this test lasted.

tiles.cap: Two companies, two landers, one 2028 Moon landing. NASA will pick whichever is ready.
tiles.nums: the first missions target two Moonwalks of about two hours each, collecting samples and testing spacesuits
tiles.p1: NASA says it and its two lander builders, Blue Origin and SpaceX, have streamlined their designs to put astronauts on the Moon in 2028. Each landing works the same way: astronauts launch in Orion on the SLS rocket from Kennedy Space Center in Florida, a commercial lander links up with Orion, two crew members go down to the surface and two stay in Orion. Which company lands first will depend on whose lander is ready.
tiles.p2: Published Friday 23 October. Artemis III, next year, is now a docking demonstration: test versions of each lander will rendezvous and dock with Orion in low Earth orbit.
deep: SpaceX’s plan: fill up in orbit

Several Starship “tanker” flights carry cryogenic propellant to a “depot” Starship waiting in low Earth orbit, which then fuels the lander. The Starship lander waits for Orion in Earth orbit, they dock, and the lander itself makes the burn that sends the stack to low lunar orbit. NASA is modifying Orion so Starship can push it to the Moon.
Blue Origin’s plan: three stages, no refuelling

For 2028, Blue Origin skips propellant transfer. Three transfer stages launch into low Earth orbit, then the Blue Moon Mark 2 lander; after docking, the stack heads to an elliptical polar orbit around the Moon, each stage dropping away as its propellant runs out. The crew moves into the lander and descends to the Moon’s South Pole.
What changed

Landers and Orion will no longer meet in a near-rectilinear halo orbit; each partner uses its own rendezvous orbit. Both companies must fly an uncrewed demonstration with their crewed landers first, and NASA certifies each lander before anyone rides it.
On the surface

The first missions target two Moonwalks of about two hours each, to collect samples and test spacesuits from Axiom Space. Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager, says the teams have been “working hand in hand to ensure we can return American astronauts to the Moon by 2028.”

tiles.cap: A 1,550 km² iceberg has drifted 2,300 km from Antarctica and just bumped into an island.
tiles.nums: area of iceberg A-81, now bumping along the underwater shelf of South Georgia
tiles.p1: Iceberg A-81 broke off Antarctica’s Brunt Ice Shelf in January 2023. It spent more than three years in the Weddell Sea, carried along the coast by the clockwise Weddell Gyre, reached the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula in May 2026, then moved north into the Scotia Sea. By late October it had reached South Georgia, a remote island in the South Atlantic about 2,300 km north-northwest of where it started. NASA’s Terra satellite photographed it there on 20 October.
tiles.p2: NASA Earth Observatory’s Image of the Day for Tuesday 27 October. In the days before the photo its progress slowed; Jan Lieser of Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology and Christopher Shuman, retired from the University of Maryland, say it appears to be bumping along the edge of the island’s underwater shelf.
deep: The crack that took 35 years
Chasm 1, the rift that released A-81, was relatively stable for about 35 years, began growing again around 2012 and by 2019 looked likely to break. It held on for several more years.
The same trap
In 2025 iceberg A-23A ran aground on the same shelf off South Georgia and later broke apart.
The ones behind it

Brunt has shed several large icebergs lately. A-74 calved from the North Rift in 2021 and has since broken up. A-83 calved from the Halloween Crack in 2024, is still intact and is trailing A-81 northward with other icebergs apparently leaving the Weddell Sea.
Who lives on Brunt

The British Antarctic Survey’s Halley Research Station has been on the Brunt Ice Shelf since the 1950s. The image came from the MODIS instrument on Terra; the iceberg data cited come from the U.S. National Ice Center’s Antarctic Iceberg Files.

tiles.cap: NTU’s 14th satellite is up, carrying the first Singapore-made solar module to fly in orbit
tiles.nums: satellites NTU has launched since X-SAT in 2011; CRIMSON-1 went up on 1 October
tiles.p1: CRIMSON-1 launched on Thursday 1 October on a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, on the Transporter-18 rideshare, and was pushed out into low Earth orbit by Exolaunch’s EXOpod Nova deployer. It carries several next-generation perovskite solar cells developed by NTU researchers with Singfilm Solar, an NUS spin-off, including a flexible perovskite module on ultrathin glass, the first Singapore-made solar module flown in orbit. The job: measure how well the cells’ durability and efficiency survive the trip from ground to space, and how much power they make up there.
tiles.p2: NTU news release 2 October. It is one of the first projects backed by the National Space Agency of Singapore under its Space Access Programme.
deep: The other experiment: thinking on board

CRIMSON-1 also carries an edge AI image-processing system. Instead of sending every raw image down a limited radio link, it processes images in orbit and sends less. Researchers will watch how the computer handles heat and power under heavy workloads.
Why perovskites
NTU’s landmark Science paper on perovskite solar cells came out in 2013. The cells are thin and light.
The one before
VELOX-AM, NTU’s 13th satellite, launched in July 2023 and deorbited in August 2026.
Who paid, who helped

Singapore’s government has put S$210 million into the Space Technology Development Programme since 2022. IMDA secured the satellite’s radio spectrum and orbital resources from the ITU; Exolaunch handled launch capacity, mission management, integration and deployment.

tiles.cap: A laptop that ships with its own screwdriver. Every part is meant to come out.
tiles.nums: battery; Tom’s Guide measured 16 h 48 min of use, Framework claims up to 20 h
tiles.p1: The Framework Laptop 13 Pro is built so the owner can replace or upgrade almost everything: memory on an LPCAMM2 module, the storage, the display, the battery, the bezel, and four slide-in expansion cards that decide which ports the laptop has. One Torx T5 screwdriver is all it needs, and it comes in the box. The chassis is CNC-machined aluminium, the 13.5-inch touchscreen runs 2880 by 1920 pixels at up to 700 nits and 30 to 120 Hz, and the trackpad is haptic.
tiles.p2: TIME Best Inventions 2026. From US$1,199 for the DIY edition. CEO Nirav Patel’s comparison: it is more like a bicycle, every part easy to replace.
deep: The port trick

Instead of fixed ports, four expansion card slots take small cards; a card can add Ethernet or HDMI in place of a USB-C port. Tom’s Guide’s unit had two USB-C and two USB-A. Change your mind, swap a card.
The numbers inside

As tested: Intel Core Ultra X7 385H, Intel Arc B390 graphics, 32 GB of memory, 1 TB SSD, Wi-Fi 7. Geekbench 6.7: 2,836 single-core and 14,715 multi-core, against 4,288 and 17,926 for a 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5. Battery test: 16 hours 48 minutes. 11.67 by 9 by 0.62 inches, 3.17 lb with all four cards in.
Old laptop, new parts

Owners of the original Laptop 13 can fit parts from the 13 Pro, though the bottom panel has to be swapped to fit the larger battery. A pop-up nodule under the keyboard deck makes opening the chassis easier than on the older model.
What reviewers found wrong

Price. Memory costs have jumped: Tom’s Guide cites LPCAMM2 modules at US$800 for 32 GB and US$1,600 for 64 GB, and the tested pre-built model went from US$2,099 at launch to US$2,899. In August every configuration was on pre-order and not shipping until November, most new parts were at least six months away, the webcam is grainy with no infrared camera for face login, the single fan means it should not be pushed hard, and the plastic bezel, held on by magnets, feels flimsy.
tiles.src: Framework · Tom’s Guide review, 2 Aug 2026 · TIME Best Inventions 2026

tiles.cap: Apple’s folding iPhone is 5.2 mm thin open. The crease is there; you just can’t see it.
tiles.nums: thickness of the iPhone Duo open; 11.3 mm closed; 254 grams
tiles.p1: The iPhone Duo folds a 7.6-inch OLED screen (1878 by 2670 pixels, 430 ppi) into a passport-sized phone with a 5.4-inch outer display. Open, it is 5.2 mm thick; closed, 11.3 mm; it weighs 254 grams. The hinge cover is 3D-printed from 100% recycled titanium, the enclosure is 85% recycled titanium, and the glass is Ceramic Shield 2 on the front and Ceramic Shield on the back.
tiles.p2: TIME Best Inventions 2026. US$1,999 for 256 GB, Apple’s most expensive iPhone. TechRadar’s verdict: a fully realised folding iPhone, but Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 is lighter, thinner and slightly cheaper.
deep: Hiding the crease

Every folding screen creases where it bends. Apple’s fix is the top layer: a matte nano-texture finish on the inner display that scatters light where the crease would show. TechRadar’s Lance Ulanoff cannot see it but can still feel it with a finger. Beneath sit custom polymer sheets, the OLED panel, a couple of glass layers and a titanium backing, bonded with flexible glue so the layers can slide as the phone folds.
The hinge

TIME reports more than 100 tiny components inside the hinge. Ulanoff says it is satisfying to use and essentially disappears when the phone is open flat. Apple’s new CEO John Ternus and five other engineers filed a patent application for foldable devices back in 2011.
The numbers inside

A20 Pro chip: Geekbench 7.1 scores of 4,007 single-core and 11,363 multi-core. Both screens run at 120 Hz and up to 3,000 nits. Apple quotes up to 44 hours of video on the outer screen and 31 on the inner; TechRadar got about 14 hours of real-world use and 13 in lab testing, and a 45 W charger reached 60% in 30 minutes. Rated IP68, 6 metres for 30 minutes; the reviewer held it under a running tap.
What reviewers found wrong

254 g is about 53 g heavier than the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and nearly 2 mm thicker folded. No Face ID, only Touch ID. The 2x zoom is a crop of the 48 MP sensor, not a true telephoto lens. Some apps look stretched on the inner screen, the right-side dock on the cover screen will divide opinion, and 256 GB is thin at this price. Apple Pencil support was still to come.
tiles.src: Apple tech specs · TechRadar review, 21 Oct 2026 · TIME Best Inventions 2026

tiles.cap: Mitochondria on the move inside a leaf: this year’s best microscope pictures
tiles.nums: the year the Nikon Small World competition began
tiles.p1: Quanta Magazine has collected winners from the 2026 Nikon Small World competitions, for still images and for video. Many were made with confocal laser scanning microscopy: label the parts of a cell with fluorescent dyes, then image one depth at a time. One video, by Patrick Hickey of Hypha Research, shows green mitochondria moving among red chloroplasts inside the leaf cells of a turtle vine.
tiles.p2: Published 21 October. Every one of these is real cells or tissue, lit up by the dyes the scientists chose.
deep: Neurons by light-sheet
Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery at the Allen Institute imaged neurons in mouse brain tissue using a light-sheet fluorescence microscope they built themselves.
A gut 1.3 mm across
Gauri Kulkarni of the Wake Forest Institute for Regenerative Medicine grew human intestinal tissue in the lab, 1.3 mm of it, and imaged the network of epithelial cells that forms the gut’s barrier.
A heartbeat in colour
Yasaman Maaref at Simon Fraser University filmed human heart muscle cells: green sarcomeres and red flashes of calcium showing the contractions.
An invader

Richard Atherton of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine caught a nest of Trypanosoma cruzi, the parasite that causes Chagas disease, inside a host cell. Andrew Moore of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute filmed cells dividing in sync, actin in white and mitochondria in blue.

tiles.cap: A sickle over the throat, a padlock on the toe: a 17th-century grave built to keep her in
tiles.nums: her age at death, from the skeleton; her name is unknown, so the team calls her Zosia
tiles.p1: In 2022 archaeologists led by Dariusz Poliński of Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń dug up a grave in Pień, north-central Poland. A sickle blade was hooked over the young woman’s throat and a triangular padlock sat on the big toe of her left foot. The researchers think both were meant to protect the living by stopping her from rising. The padlock was probably there at the first burial; the sickle was likely added later, after someone disturbed the grave.
tiles.p2: Science News Explores, Tuesday 27 October, with Halloween this Saturday. It is the first known grave to use both a sickle and a padlock.
deep: Copper in the mouth
Greenish stains on her skull suggest copper objects were placed in her mouth or nose. In Polish folklore copper was thought to ward off vampiric demons called strzygi.
What her teeth and DNA say

Strontium and oxygen isotopes in her teeth suggest she grew up near Pień. Her DNA hints that her mother’s family may have come from Scandinavia. Silver and gold threads in a silk cap suggest wealth and high status. No obvious marks of injury or illness were found; DNA analysis continues.
A cemetery off the map

Pień’s cemetery appears on no maps, has no written references and lies away from the village; it may have been reserved for people rejected by society. Another grave there holds a boy buried face-down with a triangular padlock on his right foot.
Where it was published
Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports, October 2026, by Poliński and colleagues including forensic geneticist Tomasz Grzybowski.

tiles.cap: Tense? Hum. Slow breathing plus humming was linked to higher heart-rate variability
tiles.nums: people did mental maths under stress; the 12 who first wore a face-cooling mask released less cortisol
tiles.p1: Stress switches on the sympathetic nervous system: faster heart, higher blood pressure, quicker breathing. The parasympathetic system is the counterweight, and part of it runs through the vagus nerve. Science News Explores reports four ways people have tried to nudge it: slow, deep breathing; cooling the face; humming; and tapping specific spots on the skin.
tiles.p2: Published Monday 26 October. Darshan Mehta of Massachusetts General Hospital says what matters most is finding a routine you will stick with, not which one.
deep: Try now: hum

What the research showed: a pilot trial published in Physiology & Behavior in October 2025 found slow breathing plus humming went with higher heart-rate variability. The article gives no recipe, so this one is ours: breathe in, hum slowly on the way out, and keep it up for a minute. Notice what changes.
Try later: cold face

In one trial 25 people did mental arithmetic under pressure; the 12 who had first worn a face-cooling mask, mimicking a face dipped in cold water, released less cortisol and recovered from the stress faster. Scientific Reports, November 2022.
Tapping
Tapping on specific skin spots has been linked to lower stress-hormone levels and reduced heart rate and blood pressure, per a 2025 review in Frontiers in Psychology.
Who says so

Neurologist Patricio Millar Vernetti of NYU Langone Health and physical therapist Karin Steere of the University of Puget Sound are among the experts quoted. Humming and chanting also appear in some ancient spiritual traditions.

tiles.cap: Smoke over Kalimantan and Sumatra; Singapore’s haze law now reaches 20 companies
tiles.nums: Indonesian companies served Preventive Measures Notices: seven on 16 October over Sumatra fires, three on 19 October over Kalimantan
tiles.p1: Singapore cannot put out a fire in Sumatra, but its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act can reach the companies whose land is burning. NEA said on 23 October it has served Preventive Measures Notices on 10 Indonesian companies: each must deploy firefighters, stop or not start burning on its land, and submit a plan to put out or prevent fires. Ten Singapore-registered palm oil and forestry companies, among them Wilmar International, Golden Agri International and Asia Pulp & Paper, have been told to hand over information on their links to Indonesian companies, where their concessions are, and what they did to prevent fires this dry season.
tiles.p2: Tuesday 5:15 pm regional update: moderate to dense smoke haze over parts of Kalimantan, southern Sumatra, southeastern Sulawesi and southern Papua; a few stations in southern Kalimantan and Sumatra read Unhealthy to Very Unhealthy. Winds over southern ASEAN are blowing generally from the east to southeast, except over Borneo, where they vary.
deep: What satellites could see

Scattered hotspots in East Kalimantan, a few in southern Sumatra and central Sarawak. NEA notes the full extent over Kalimantan and Sumatra could not be determined because smoke and cloud hid the ground.
The outlook

Dry weather over parts of southern ASEAN, with showers over Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra, Java and parts of Borneo. Where it stays dry, hotspots and smoke haze are likely to remain elevated, with a continued risk of transboundary haze.
Monday’s numbers

Monday’s 6 pm readings were the latest NEA advisory available when this wall was written: 1-hour PM2.5 of 28 to 40 µg/m³ and a 24-hour PSI of 67 to 74, Moderate. NEA’s forecast for Tuesday was 60 to 90.
The law

Under section 9 of the Act, a Preventive Measures Notice goes to companies with fires on their land outside Singapore; under section 10, NEA can demand documents from Singapore-registered companies. NEA is also writing to the 10 Indonesian companies for documents on the fires in their concessions.

tiles.cap: The students who got their answers from AI scored 17% worse on the test
tiles.nums: on the exam, after working with a chatbot
tiles.p1: Nearly 1,000 high-school maths students in Turkey were split three ways: problem sets with a plain ChatGPT-style bot, with a version that only gave hints, or with books and notes. While the bot was there the chatbot group looked brilliant, 48% more problems right. Then the AI was taken away for the exam. They scored 17% below the students who never had it.
tiles.p2: Why: they had the answers without doing the thinking, so nothing stuck.
deep: The hint-only version was different
Students who used the tutor that refused to give answers did 127% better in the sessions and then matched the book group on the exam. Same technology, different design, opposite result.
What the researchers concluded
The problem was not AI. It was asking for the answer instead of asking for help. Hamsa Bastani, one of the authors, called the result a cautionary tale.
Try it on yourself
Next hard problem, ask only for a hint, then close the chat and finish alone. See whether you still remember it a week later. This includes the maths set-up your dad built with Claude.

tiles.cap: Mars dust clings to spacesuit cloth for years. Perseverance measured grains 100 nm wide.
tiles.nums: Martian days of dust measurements on five spacesuit swatches riding on Perseverance
tiles.p1: Perseverance carries five squares of spacesuit material, each 20 mm across, on the calibration target of its SHERLOC instrument. Over 1,645 Martian days the rover’s PIXL X-ray instrument measured the dust that settled on them and on PIXL’s own Teflon and basaltic-glass targets. It found fine particles below 2.5 micrometres and ultrafine ones around 100 nanometres, far smaller than the roughly 3 micrometres earlier Mars measurements could resolve.
tiles.p2: Published Tuesday 27 October in PNAS; lead author Scott VanBommel of Washington University in St. Louis. The findings feed into spacesuit and habitat design, dust-removal procedures and crew health standards.
deep: Static decides what sticks

Grains pick up charge as they collide in the Martian air, and static electricity appears to decide which sizes stick to which surfaces. On PIXL’s Teflon target and SHERLOC’s Vectran swatch, particles averaged about 2 micrometres; on PIXL’s basaltic glass and SHERLOC’s Teflon swatch, sizes ran down to 100 to 300 nanometres. The finest grains stayed put through years of driving and drilling.
Why size matters for lungs

On Earth, particles below 2.5 micrometres reach deep into the lungs and can enter the bloodstream. Ultrafine particles of 100 nanometres or less can travel from the nasal cavity to the brain along the olfactory nerve. Martian dust is mostly silicate minerals and includes perchlorates, which can disrupt thyroid function, and reactive iron, which can damage cells. The risk is thought to depend on how much dust and for how long.
What is in it

Chemically the dust matches the iron- and sulfur-rich composition earlier missions measured, and PIXL found it enriched in phosphorus, with signs of calcium sulfate. Mars grains are less abrasive than Moon dust, which during Apollo scratched visors, wore outer suit layers, damaged seals and gave some crew members hay-fever-like symptoms.
Designing around it

Some materials hold less dust than others, which could guide future material and coating choices. Suitports and dual-chamber airlocks could cut how much dust gets into living quarters. In March 2025 NASA tested an Electrodynamic Dust Shield on the Moon aboard Firefly Aerospace’s Blue Ghost Mission 1, using electric fields to clear regolith from glass and radiator surfaces.

tiles.cap: NASA’s Titan drone flew its whole first flight on a computer that believes it is on Titan.
tiles.nums: arrival at Titan, after launch no earlier than 2028 and a six-year voyage
tiles.p1: Dragonfly is the rotorcraft NASA will send to Saturn’s moon Titan. In a blog post on Friday 23 October NASA said the team at Johns Hopkins APL in Laurel, Maryland had run its simulated first flight, from backshell separation to landing, in real time on flight-like avionics, the most comprehensive test of that flight so far. The computer flew on simulated data from Dragonfly’s navigation cameras, inertial measurement units and lidar, covering most of the systems and manoeuvres it will use on Titan.
tiles.p2: Titan is too far for anyone on Earth to steer it live, so Dragonfly must fly itself. Next: the same flight on the real flight system, other flight profiles, and faults injected on purpose to confirm it recovers on its own.
deep: Built up one rotor at a time
The team tested incrementally: first a single rotor spinning, then a short reposition flight, then a partial scouting flight, adding sensors at each step.
Faking Titan for the cameras
A custom camera emulator renders Titan scenes on GPUs and matches the 20 to 70 millisecond exposure times of the real cameras, so the flight computer sees what it would see over the dunes.
Three years of hopping
Dragonfly launches no earlier than 2028, travels for six years and arrives in 2034. It then spends three years flying between sites on Titan.
Lowering it out of the shell

Lockheed Martin engineers are testing the mechanism that lowers the rotorcraft from its stowed position inside the backshell into position for release during descent: static load tests, deployment tests, and deployments at tilted angles.

tiles.cap: Three voters can make a loop: A beats B, B beats C, C beats A. Underneath: a Klein bottle.
tiles.nums: when Condorcet found the paradox; in 1951 Arrow proved no ranking method escapes it
tiles.p1: Split voters into three equal groups. One ranks Alice, Bob, Carol; the next Bob, Carol, Alice; the last Carol, Alice, Bob. Alice beats Bob two groups to one, Bob beats Carol, and Carol beats Alice. Every voter is perfectly consistent, yet the group’s choice runs in a circle. Nicolas de Condorcet found this in 1785, and in 1951 Kenneth Arrow proved that no ranking method can satisfy four reasonable rules at once.
tiles.p2: In 2025 Ori Livson and Mikhail Prokopenko at the University of Sydney, with Siddharth Pritam of the Chennai Mathematical Institute, showed the paradox lives on a Klein bottle: a one-sided surface with no inside, no outside and no edge.
deep: Check it yourself

Take the three rankings above and compare each pair. Alice vs Bob: groups 1 and 3 prefer Alice. Bob vs Carol: groups 1 and 2 prefer Bob. Carol vs Alice: groups 2 and 3 prefer Carol. Three majorities, one loop.
Ballots as triangles

In 1993 Yuliy Baryshnikov drew each of the six possible rankings as a triangle, one corner for each pairwise comparison. Rankings that agree on two comparisons share an edge, so the six triangles glue into a strip, and the strip’s matching ends bend round into a tube. That tube gave a topological proof of Arrow’s theorem.
The rims he ignored

One rim of the tube reads Alice over Bob, Bob over Carol, Carol over Alice; the other runs the cycle backwards. Both are Condorcet loops. Gluing the rims straight pairs up incompatible rankings; gluing with a twist works. Livson: “Gluing with the twist is the only valid option.” Twist a strip and join it and you get a Möbius strip; twist a tube and join it and you get a Klein bottle.
Arrow’s four rules

Voters may rank candidates in any order. No single voter dictates the outcome. If everyone prefers one option to another, the group ranking agrees. And how two candidates rank should depend only on how voters compare those two. Iain McLean of Oxford: “It’s not really a mathematical debate. It’s a debate about values.”
